title: Simple Bank System
statement:
Design a class `Bank` that runs transactions on `n` accounts numbered `1` to `n`, where account `i + 1` starts with `balance[i]` dollars.

A transaction goes through only if every account number it names is between `1` and `n`, and, for a withdrawal or a transfer, the account paying out holds at least `money` dollars. A transaction that goes through updates the balances and returns `true`; one that does not changes nothing and returns `false`.

- `Bank(balance)` sets up the accounts from the array `balance`.
- `transfer(account1, account2, money)` moves `money` dollars from account `account1` to account `account2`.
- `deposit(account, money)` adds `money` dollars to account `account`.
- `withdraw(account, money)` removes `money` dollars from account `account`.
constraints: At most 10^4 calls are made to each of transfer, deposit and withdraw

signature.name: Bank
methods: boolean transfer(int account1, int account2, long money)

notes:
## Intuition

This is a straight simulation: keep every account's balance in an array and, for each call, decide whether the transaction is allowed before touching anything. Only two things can make a call fail: an account number outside `1..n`, or a paying account that holds less than `money`. Checking both first means a failed call never leaves a half-done change behind.

## Approach

1. Copy `balance` into `this.balance` and remember `n`. Account `a` lives at index `a - 1`.
2. `exists(account)` says whether `account` is between `1` and `n`.
3. `transfer`: fail if either account does not exist, or if account `account1` has less than `money`; otherwise subtract from one balance, add to the other and succeed.
4. `deposit`: fail if the account does not exist; otherwise add `money`.
5. `withdraw`: fail if the account does not exist or holds less than `money`; otherwise subtract it.

## Example 1, step by step

Balances start at `[10, 100, 20, 50, 30]`. `withdraw(3, 10)`: account 3 holds 20, so it drops to 10 and the call returns `true`. `transfer(5, 1, 20)`: account 5 holds 30, so it drops to 10 and account 1 rises to 30: `true`. `deposit(5, 20)` brings account 5 to 30: `true`. `transfer(3, 4, 15)`: account 3 holds only 10, so `false`. `withdraw(10, 50)`: there are only 5 accounts, so `false`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) per call (O(n) once to copy `balance`).
- Space: O(n) for the balances.

## Pitfalls

- Account numbers start at 1, the array at 0: always index with `account - 1`.
- In `transfer`, check that both accounts exist before moving any money; otherwise money could vanish into an account that does not exist.
- Paying out exactly the whole balance is allowed (`<` fails, `<=` succeeds); so is moving `0`, and transferring to the same account.
- Balances can grow past 32-bit range, so Java needs `long`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `this.balance` | current balance of each account, account `a` at index `a - 1` |
| `this.n` | number of accounts |
| `account`, `account1`, `account2` | account numbers named by a call |
| `money` | the amount the call moves |
